W7224362461.abstract: Knowledge editing for large language models typically treats a fact update as a replacement in which a new object overwrites the old.Many real-world facts, however, evolve through sequences: the same subject-relation pair maps to different objects across disjoint intervals, each correct within its validity window.Existing temporal-editing benchmarks probe latestvalue or explicit-time recall, so they cannot determine whether an edited model retains a coherent timeline.We introduce TKE-BENCH, a diagnostic benchmark that operationalizes temporal accessibility along three reasoningoriented axes with paraphrased variants.On TKE-BENCH, all evaluated editing baselines collapse on chronologically structured queries, revealing catastrophic temporal interference (CTI).We trace CTI to a geometric property implicit in locate-and-edit methods: mid-layer subject-token keys are nearly collinear across time slices of the same subject, so stacked updates write along one direction and the latest edit overwrites every earlier value.Building on this, we propose CHRONOEXPERT, a temporal mixture-of-experts that stores each time slice in an independent lightweight expert and activates only the matching one at inference, leaving the base model otherwise untouched.Across multiple LLM backbones, CHRONOEXPERT consistently outperforms the strongest editing baselines and stays robust as chains grow longer.

W7224429474.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently hallucinate when confronted with queries they cannot answer reliably.The root causes are multifaceted, including entity rarity, semantic ambiguity, temporal invalidity, false presuppositions, and other forms of epistemic uncertainty.Existing abstention mechanisms overwhelmingly rely on binary probes trained with manually curated "unanswerable" labels or calibrated confidence scores, both of which presuppose access to negative examples that are expensive to collect and fundamentally incomplete in coverage.We propose FLOW-ABSTAIN, an unsupervised framework that reframes queryaware abstention as density estimation in the model's own latent space.Our method operates in three stages: (1) extracting intermediate hidden-state representations from a curated set of confidently answerable queries, (2) applying PCA-based dimensionality reduction to obtain a compact manifold, and (3) fitting a Masked Autoregressive Flow (MAF) to the resulting representations, yielding an exact, tractable log-likelihood for arbitrary new inputs.At inference time, queries whose latent projections receive low log-likelihood under the learned density are flagged for abstention-without requiring any negative or out-of-distribution training samples.Experiments across three instruction-tuned LLMs (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Llama3-8B-Instruct) and five diverse evaluation benchmarks demonstrate that FLOW-ABSTAIN achieves highly competitive abstention performance among methods with practical inference cost while providing a continuous, interpretable likelihood signal that naturally stratifies query difficulty along cognitive dimensions of unanswerability. 1

W7224464424.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly required to process inputs composed of multiple context units, such as answer options, retrieved passages, or in-context demonstrations.Effective reasoning in such scenarios demands capturing both intrinsic semantics within each unit and the aggregated semantics across units.However, recent efforts typically treat multiple units as a single entangled sequence, ignoring the distinct knowledge within isolated units, which leads to suboptimal performance.To this end, we propose MUA 1 (Multiple Context Units Attention), a dual-view self-attention module that computes a local view for learning unit-specific semantics and a global view to enable bidirectional interaction across units.These two views share projection matrices and are fused by a lightweight input-conditioned gate, while generation proceeds with standard causal decoding.With an optimized implementation, this design achieves efficient fusion of multiple context units and superior information utilization during input encoding at marginal overhead.Experiments on diverse multiple context units reasoning benchmarks, including multiple-choice, multi-hop QA and language understanding tasks, show that MUA consistently improves performance across model scales, exhibits increased robustness to context units reordering, and establishes new state-of-the-art results on key benchmarks.

W7224524270.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly act through tools, APIs, databases, and other stateful environments, where task success depends on external evidence rather than final text alone.Existing reward paradigms face a trade-off: preference and rubric-based feedback are flexible but often weakly grounded, while verifier-based rewards are grounded but typically tied to narrow task-specific checkers.We argue that agentic reinforcement learning needs reward interfaces: mechanisms that explicitly connect task requirements to environment evidence, provenance, and reward aggregation.We introduce Agentic Rubrics, an executable reward-interface view with four components: criteria, evidence acquisition, provenance, and aggregation.This view separates what should be evaluated from how evidence is obtained, audited, and converted into reward.In this case study, Agentic Rubrics augment final environment feedback with process-aware rewards derived from tool traces and state records, yielding modest improvements in task performance and process reliability while revealing domain-dependent limitations.These results support the position that grounded agent learning should treat reward construction as an interface problem, not only as scalar reward modeling. Pure Rubric Verifier Agentic RubricCorrect acceptance: process constraints and state transitions are both verified.

W7224879143.abstract: The growing demand for artificial intelligence systems that are responsive, privacy-preserving, and capable of operating autonomously is driving the adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) on edge devices. However, deploying LLMs as the core of agents on devices with limited resources still faces computational and memory constraints. This research develops an LLM-based local agent architecture that runs locally on a Raspberry Pi without relying on cloud services. The system integrates local LLM inference with agentic functions, including intent processing, reasoning, tool invocation, and interaction with hardware via GPIO. Several quantized Small Language Models (SLMs) were evaluated on a Raspberry Pi 5 with 16 GB of RAM using CPU-based inference. The evaluation included total latency, Time to First Token (TTFT), token generation rate, peak RAM usage, peak CPU utilization, and peak temperature. The results showed significant performance differences among the models. Qwen 2.5 0.5B Q3 produced the lowest total latency of 23.9 seconds, the lowest TTFT of 269.0 ms, and the highest generation rate of 12.1 tokens/s. However, the results indicate that inference speed alone is not sufficient to determine the most suitable model as the core of a local agent. Most models reached peak CPU utilization above 95%, while RAM usage and thermal characteristics varied across configurations. Based on a combination of inference performance and resource usage, models in the 1B–1.7B range specifically LLaMA 3.2 1B Q4, Qwen 2.5 1.5B Q4, and SmolLM 1.7B Q4 show potential as a balanced set of candidates between responsiveness and model capacity. The research results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying LLMs as local agents on low-cost edge devices and provide a basis for selecting models based on a balance between inference efficiency, resource constraints, and agentic capabilities.

W7224975610.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in settings where outputs are grounded in cited sources, yet whether citation presence itself, independent of factual content, shapes model behavior remains poorly understood. We introduce AuthorityBench, a benchmark of 220,564 prompts designed to isolate the effect of citation presence on factual accuracy in large language models. Citations appear passively in prompts, models receive no instruction to trust or defer to them, allowing us to measure whether citation presence alone cause models to give wrong answers. The benchmark independently manipulates two variables: whether the claim is true or false, and whether the accompanying citation is real or fabricated. This yields four conditions tested across four domains (general knowledge, science, law, and medicine), with controlled variation over 40 prompt templates, four venue prestige tiers, and author names from six surname regions. We define hallucination as any response contradicting the ground-truth label, wrongly denying a true claim or wrongly affirming a false one, capturing both the familiar failure of endorsing misinformation and the novel failure of rejecting correct facts under authority pressure; refused responses are excluded from this count. Across all seven models, adding any citation, real or fabricated, increases hallucination above baseline. The effect is largest when a fabricated citation accompanies a true claim: models that answer correctly without a citation are pushed toward wrong answers by the authority signal alone, with hallucination rates rising 3 to 22 percentage points and reaching 35--77% in general knowledge. Legal claims are consistently robust; venue prestige and author demographics have negligible effects; and larger models are no more resistant than smaller ones. All code, datasets, prompt templates, and evaluation resources are available at https://github.com/aryank2804/AuthorityBench.

W7225150811.abstract: Conclusions in power-system research require a clear evidential basis. Researchers need to understand the data sources, modelling assumptions, and solution procedures to assess the conditions under which a conclusion holds. Large language models (LLMs) can help researchers extract information from documents and translate research requests into code and tool calls, but their outputs still require physical validation. Focusing on human-supervised artificial intelligence (AI) researchers, this review examines power-system LLM applications and related scientific workflows, together with physics-grounded power AI studies, to discuss the conditions for using LLMs in scientific research. In the proposed knowledge-physics-simulation-governance framework, LLMs translate information and coordinate tasks, simulators and validation tools test models, and experts retain authority over critical assumptions, safety boundaries, and final conclusions. Research processes should preserve materials for review so that claims can be traced to their sources, computations can be reproduced, and failed attempts and approvals can be examined. On this basis, a staged development roadmap and requirements for research reporting are proposed. Evaluation should focus on research artifacts and their validation to assess whether LLMs can improve the efficiency of power-system research within clearly defined permissions.

W7225155615.abstract: Current polymers used for carbon capture are limited by their toxic footprint during manufacturing and degradation over time. This review aims to propose a new paradigm for designing membranes for carbon dioxide capture using data-driven approaches to bibliometrics, artificial intelligence, and machine learning with the goal of creating next-generation, sustainable polymers for carbon dioxide capture. Bibliometric analysis using VOSviewer and Bibliometrix will be used to present the most commonly used keywords, people, and countries that are working more on this topic. Furthermore, an exposing of the gaps between the performance of membranes under laboratory settings versus in real world environments will be conducted. AI and machine learning approaches will be investigated to fill these performance gaps. Methods for shifting towards a circular economy with the inverse design of bio based polymers, green fillers, and low carbon, non toxic solvents will be discussed. Finally, the virtual discoveries in the field of polymers for carbon capture will be correlated with the current industrial world to formulate a roadmap for these materials to reach high technology readiness levels for use across the globe.

W7225162656.abstract: An investigation into why a unit of business work did not finish in a distributed operational pipeline crosses several systems of record: schedulers, orchestration engines, warehouses, code repositories and configuration stores. This monograph formulates Contract-Bounded Agent Design (CBAD), a reproducible engineering method for building language-model agents that conduct such investigations within fixed boundaries and can be carried from one pipeline to the next. The method rests on four structural decisions: one narrow, read-only tool per external source, whose description serves as a semantic contract; safety contracts enforced in code, including statement guards, pinned query scopes, payload ceilings and truncation reported with true totals; an explicit failure taxonomy that classifies by meaning on two orthogonal axes, the business stage at which work stopped and the concern that owns the fix; and a named separation between the current state of the work and its historical occurrence. Around the decisions the book sets an ordered investigation runbook, an answer discipline that limits each answer to what the tools returned, and four named design rules: liveness check before trust, best-effort secondary write, partial success by construction and routing by identifier shape. The decisions were derived from two systems developed separately in the author’s own practice as a software engineer, an incident-investigation agent over a workflow orchestration engine and a multi-purpose assistant over a scheduled data pipeline, and the graded convergence of their designs is the principal evidence for the method. The method is positioned against research on tool-using agents, AIOps and failure management, natural-language interfaces to data, software architecture and technical debt. Its procedures are given as checklists, decision tables and rule cards, worked through on a constructed claims-processing pipeline, and the final chapter adds a transfer checklist and a staged adoption path. The book addresses software engineers, site reliability engineers and architects who build, review or adopt agents over production workflow and data systems.

W7225172179.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the com putational cost of large language models (LLMs), but it can introduce internal structural and behavioral changes that are not captured by traditional metrics such as accuracy and per plexity. We present TopoQuant, a topological framework that uses topological data analysis (TDA) to quantify structural drift in self-attention weights and relate it to behavioral changes in quantized LLMs. Across four LLM families and multiple quantization levels, we show that topological drift remains stable at moderate compression levels but increases sharply below 4 bit precision, closely tracking declines in attention agreement. Our results reveal a strong relationship between topological drift and attention agreement, indicating that structural changes in model parameters closely reflect behavioral degradation under quantization. We further demonstrate that topological features can accurately predict attention consistency using lightweight machine learning models, achieving R2 scores of up to 0.85. Predicting attention agreement enables efficient assessment of be havioral consistency in quantized LLMs, allowing quantization induced degradation to be detected without running expensive downstream tasks. The results indicate that topological drift pro vides an efficient early-warning signal for quantization-induced degradation and can help identify safe compression limits without extensive downstream evaluation.

W7225242799.abstract: Edge analytics requires continuous model adaptation under tight latency, bandwidth, and confidentiality constraints, yet conventional federated learning can leak sensitive information through shared updates and often struggles under non-IID client data. This study introduces Federated Quantum Machine Learning that transmits privacy-preserving measurement statistics derived from hybrid parameterized quantum circuits rather than raw samples or high-dimensional gradients. Across 50 edge clients over 20 rounds, the proposed method achieves 0.844 accuracy and 0.836 macro-F1 with ECE 0.048, outperforming a classical FedAvg baseline (0.801 accuracy, 0.788 macro-F1, ECE 0.062) while maintaining predictable edge overhead (845 ms average round latency) and compact messaging (3.1 KB average payload per round). Privacy–measurement sweeps demonstrate accuracy saturation with increasing privacy budget, improving from 0.816 at ε = 0.5 to 0.856 at ε = 8.0 under 512 shots, while calibration improves more sharply, with ECE decreasing from 0.068 to 0.046 over the same range. Increasing shot budget from 128 to 2048 consistently increases accuracy under all privacy settings, confirming that measurement variance is a controllable bottleneck for protected learning. Communication analysis shows that statistics-only messaging remains an order of magnitude smaller than gradient-style baselines (33.9 KB average payload per round), and secure aggregation adds bounded overhead (4.8 KB average payload) with a modest utility shift (0.836 accuracy, ECE 0.051). Robustness experiments under severe non-IID drift (severity 0.9) preserve macro-F1 at 0.801 with expectation-based statistics versus 0.772 for histogram-based statistics, and perturbed-client tests show improved stability with robust aggregation, sustaining 0.836 accuracy at 10% perturbed participation compared to 0.824 under naïve aggregation. These results indicate that low-dimensional, privatized measurement summaries enable practical, reliable, and privacy-aligned federated quantum learning on constrained edge infrastructures.

W7225255302.abstract: As autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents transition from passive credit scoring and fraud classification to executing multi-step decision chains in safety-critical financial environments—such as high-frequency algorithmic market making, automated anti-money laundering (AML) asset freezing, cross-border settlement, and dynamic liquidity management—ensuring high precision alongside absolute risk compliance becomes paramount. Traditional statistical validation, backtesting, and empirical stress-testing fall short when confronting the inherent opacity, non-determinism, and infinite state spaces of generative models and deep neural controllers. A single hallucinated transaction parameter set, unauthorized logic branch, or out-of-distribution execution can trigger systemic market instability, severe regulatory non-compliance, or irreversible capital destruction. This paper presents a novel Financial Hybrid Verification Architecture (Fin-HVA) designed to mathematically certify the correctness, policy compliance, and risk bounds of autonomous agent decision sequences prior to market execution. We introduce a neuro-symbolic semantic parser that converts complex natural language reasoning and tool-use parameter arrays into formal Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas and Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) queries. By coupling static SMT reachability solvers with a real-time Runtime Financial Safety Shield (RFSS) and an autonomous evaluator-optimizer repair loop, Fin-HVA guarantees that agent decisions remain strictly bounded within predefined risk envelopes (e.g., maximum drawdown thresholds, capital adequacy ratios, and regulatory compliance constraints). We evaluate Fin-HVA across three simulated high-risk financial domains: automated high-frequency algorithmic liquidity management, dynamic credit line adjustment, and real-time AML transaction interdiction. Our experimental results demonstrate that Fin-HVA completely eliminates safety and compliance violations (0.0% Violation Rate) while maintaining high operational task success rates (>94%) with negligible step latency (<1.3s). This research establishes a rigorous mathematical foundation for deploying fully autonomous AI agents within highly regulated financial ecosystems.

W7225256512.abstract: Predicting patient response to cancer treatments remains a challenge due to tumor heterogeneity and complex tumor microenvironments (TMEs). Modern spatial genomics technologies enable gene expression profiling alongside histological frameworks, but comprehensive analysis and clinical translation of these high-dimensionality datasets will benefit from Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). This review synthesizes computational approaches that address challenges of spatial data by examining deep-learning architectures such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for histological feature extraction and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for modeling cell-cell interactions. We then explore the paradigm of Foundation Models that bridge histopathology with transcriptomics to accelerate the identification of spatially resolved biomarkers, improve patient stratification for immunotherapy and targeted treatments, and advance the clinical translation of mechanistic insights derived from the tumor microenvironment.

W7225299146.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by high postoperative recurrence and marked heterogeneity.Conventional imaging and serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) are insufficient for precise prognostic assessment and recurrence monitoring.Liquid biopsy, especially circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), can noninvasively reflect tumor genomic alterations and minimal residual disease (MRD), often predicting recurrence 2~5 months earlier than imaging.Radiomics and deep learning can extract high-throughput quantitative features from CT/MRI, reflecting spatial heterogeneity, microvascular invasion (MVI), and the immune microenvironment.Integrating spatial imaging information with temporal molecular information from liquid biopsy into "imaging-genomics" or multimodal fusion models can improve diagnostic accuracy, recurrence risk stratification, and therapeutic monitoring.This review systematically summarizes the integrated application of multimodal imaging and liquid biopsy in HCC prognosis and recurrence monitoring.It further emphasizes fusion methodology, including early fusion versus late fusion and their respective advantages and disadvantages, algorithm-specific challenges, HCC etiological heterogeneity (especially NAFLD/MASH-related HCC), controversies and unresolved issues, and specific head-to-head trial designs.Finally, we discuss artificial intelligence, prospective trials, and full-course management.

W7225394258.abstract: Commercialization of lithium metal batteries with high energy density is limited largely due to uncontrolled lithium dendrite growth, poor interfacial resistance of solid-state electrolytes, and inadequate cycle stability of solid-state electrolytes. A new architecture that leverages artificial intelligence to design engineered nanolayer interfaces for solid-state electrolytes enables controlled lithium-ion transport and prevents dendrite propagation in next-generation batteries. To achieve this, the proposed framework combines Multiphysics interfacial modeling with an artificial intelligence optimization module to simultaneously determine the optimal thickness and interfacial parameters for nanolayers to optimize ionic conductivity while minimizing electrochemical degradation. Simulation results show that the engineered interface provides a significantly better electrochemical performance than any existing solid-state electrolyte configuration. The engineered interface provides an ionic conductivity of 1.21 × 10−3 S·cm−1, an improvement of approximately 34.8%, and a decrease in interfacial resistance of 82 Ω·cm² to 46 Ω·cm², a decrease of 43.9%, and a critical current density of 2.1 mA·cm−2 compared to an average critical current density of 1.3 mA·cm−2 demonstrating greater tolerance to dendrites. Long-term cycle testing indicates that the proposed configuration retains 93.4% capacity after 500 cycles, while the conventional interface retains only 79.6% of its capacity when cycled under equivalent conditions. Collectively, these results indicate that the combination of nanolayer engineering and artificial intelligence optimization enables uniform deposition of lithium ions, enhances interfacial stability, and reduces the degree of dendrite-induced degradation. The proposed framework enables large-scale development of safer, long-lasting solid-state lithium-ion batteries and facilitates high-energy-density storage for electric vehicles and large renewable energy systems
